analysis.investment_thesis: NephroPlus operates in an extraordinarily underpenetrated market — India treats only ~15-20% of its CKD patients requiring dialysis — giving the company a multi-decade secular growth runway with near-inelastic demand. At 27.5% revenue CAGR and rapidly improving unit economics, this is a genuine growth story, but profitability is too nascent and ROE too modest for a high-conviction Fisher buy today.
key_strengths: Exceptional TAM with structural underpenetration: dialysis is non-discretionary (3x/week per patient), recurring revenue, near-zero churn once enrolled
Accelerating operating leverage: operating income CAGR 45.8% vs. revenue CAGR 27.5%; operating margin expanded from ~13% (FY21) to 22%+ (FY25)
Geographically diversified growth engine (India, Saudi Arabia, Philippines, Uzbekistan, Nepal) with strong 63.85% promoter alignment
key_risks: ROE of only 13.4% well below Fisher's 20% threshold — dialysis centers are capital-intensive with long payback periods
Net profit only turned positive in FY24; losses in FY22/FY23 mean the earnings track record is thin and FCF only modestly positive (INR 35 Cr in FY25 vs. INR 101 Cr capex)
Trailing P/E of 74.7x leaves no room for execution missteps; any deceleration in new center ramp-ups would reprice the stock severely
red_flags: Net losses as recently as FY22 (−INR 21 Cr) and FY23 (−INR 12 Cr) — management has yet to prove a full economic cycle of profitability
Heavy and rising capex (INR 80 Cr → INR 101 Cr FY24→FY25) keeps FCF generation thin relative to the growth narrative
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From the scuttlebutt perspective, NephroPlus is building what could become a dominant national dialysis network in a country where renal care infrastructure is desperately inadequate. Revenue has grown from INR 286 Cr to INR 756 Cr in four years at 27.5% CAGR — squarely in Fisher territory — and the operating leverage is visible: EBIT margin has nearly tripled from ~13% to ~22% as fixed center costs get absorbed. The delivery model innovation (home hemodialysis, dialysis on wheels, holiday dialysis) suggests management is thinking about the business the way Fisher would admire — constantly expanding the service envelope to capture a larger share of patient lifetime value. Finance costs are modest (D/E 0.36), and the INR 126 Cr cash position provides adequate runway.

The hesitation is earnings quality and return on capital. Fisher demanded companies that could deploy capital at high returns — here ROE sits at just 13.4% and ROCE at 14.1%, both well below the 20% bar, reflecting the reality that each new dialysis center requires INR 1-2 Cr of upfront equipment and fit-out before generating returns over 5-7 years. Net profit was negative as recently as FY23, and cumulative FCF over five years is barely breakeven. The forward P/E of 28x is genuinely reasonable *if* the company compounds earnings at 30%+ annually — but that is a big "if" for a business with fewer than three profitable years. I would want to see two more years of 20%+ ROE improvement before moving this to a conviction BUY.
